Let \(S=S_L\). Since \(L\) is Lagrangian, \(S\) is symmetric. Since \(\jmath(L)=L\), \(S\) commutes with the diagonal sign matrix
\[
\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,1,-1),
\]
so entries with opposite parity indices vanish. With the imposed conditions,
\[
S=\begin{pmatrix}
1&0&a&0\\
0&b&0&0\\
a&0&c&0\\
0&0&0&1
\end{pmatrix},
\]
where
\[
a=s_{13},\qquad b=s_{22},\qquad c=s_{33}.
\]
Thus
\[
A_L=c,\qquad B_L=b+2a.
\]
Write
\[
A=c,\qquad B=b+2a.
\]
Then \(b=B-2a\), so counting \(L\) is the same as counting triples \((a,A,B)\in\mathbb F_q^3\) satisfying the displayed conditions.

For \(x\in E\), put \(w=x+Sx\in L\). The \(E\)-component of \(\rho_t(w)\) is
\[
x-\bigl(x_1+\ell_t(Sx)\bigr)v_t,
\]
where
\[
\ell_t(y_1f_1+\cdots+y_4f_4)=y_1+ty_2+t^2y_3+t^3y_4.
\]
Hence \(\rho_t(L)\cap F=0\) iff the rank-one map
\[
x\mapsto x-\bigl(x_1+\ell_t(Sx)\bigr)v_t
\]
is invertible. Its determinant is
\[
-\ell_t(Sv_t).
\]
Now
\[
Sv_t=(1+at^2)f_1+btf_2+(a+ct^2)f_3+t^3f_4,
\]
so
\[
\ell_t(Sv_t)=1+(2a+b)t^2+ct^4+t^6
=1+Bt^2+At^4+t^6.
\]
Thus the condition is
\[
g(u):=u^3+Au^2+Bu+1\neq 0
\]
for every square \(u=t^2\in\mathbb F_q\). Since \(g(0)=1\), this means \(g\) has no nonzero square root in \(\mathbb F_q\).

The condition
\[
a^2=A^2B^2-A^3-B^3
\]
is exactly
\[
a^2=\operatorname{disc}(g),
\]
because in characteristic \(3\),
\[
\operatorname{disc}(u^3+Au^2+Bu+1)=A^2B^2-A^3-B^3.
\]
For each \(g\), the number of possible \(a\)'s is \(2\) if the discriminant is a nonzero square, \(1\) if it is \(0\), and \(0\) otherwise.

For separable cubics over \(\mathbb F_q\), the discriminant is a square exactly when Frobenius acts by an even permutation on the three roots. Hence the contributing separable cubics are exactly:

- irreducible cubics, Frobenius a \(3\)-cycle;
- split cubics with three distinct roots in \(\mathbb F_q\).

The noncontributing separable cubics are linear times irreducible quadratic.

First count irreducible cubics \(g\) with constant term \(1\). If \(\alpha\in\mathbb F_{q^3}\) is a root, then
\[
\operatorname{Norm}_{\mathbb F_{q^3}/\mathbb F_q}(\alpha)=-1.
\]
The norm fiber has size
\[
q^2+q+1.
\]
Among these elements, exactly one lies in \(\mathbb F_q\), namely \(-1\), since \(x^3=-1\) has the unique solution \(x=-1\) in characteristic \(3\). Therefore the number of degree \(3\) elements is \(q^2+q\), and each irreducible cubic has \(3\) roots, so
\[
N_{\mathrm{irr}}=\frac{q^2+q}{3}.
\]
Each contributes weight \(2\), giving
\[
2N_{\mathrm{irr}}=\frac{2q(q+1)}{3}.
\]

Now consider split cubics with three distinct roots. Their roots \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in\mathbb F_q^\times\) satisfy
\[
\alpha\beta\gamma=-1.
\]
They are allowed only if none of the roots is a square, so all three roots must be nonsquares. A product of three nonsquares is nonsquare, so this is possible exactly when \(-1\) is nonsquare, i.e. when \(r\) is odd.

Assume \(r\) is odd. Let
\[
n=\frac{q-1}{2}
\]
be the number of nonsquares. Counting unordered triples of distinct nonsquares with product \(-1\) is equivalent to counting unordered triples of distinct elements of the square subgroup \(H\), of order \(n\), with prescribed product. Since \(n\) is odd and not divisible by \(3\), the number is
\[
\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}{6}.
\]
Each such cubic contributes weight \(2\), so the split contribution is
\[
\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}{3}.
\]

Finally count repeated-root cubics with no square root in \(\mathbb F_q\). The triple-root case is
\[
g(u)=(u+1)^3,
\]
whose root is \(-1\), allowed exactly when \(r\) is odd. The double-root case has
\[
g(u)=(u-\lambda)^2(u-\mu),\qquad \lambda^2\mu=-1.
\]
Both roots must be nonsquares. This again happens exactly when \(r\) is odd, and then \(\lambda\) may be any nonsquare except \(-1\), giving \(n-1\) cases. Including the triple-root case gives repeated contribution
\[
n
\]
when \(r\) is odd, and \(0\) when \(r\) is even.

Therefore
\[
M_r=\frac{2q(q+1)}{3}
\]
if \(r\) is even, while if \(r\) is odd,
\[
M_r=\frac{2q(q+1)}{3}+\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}{3}+n.
\]
Since \(n=(q-1)/2\),
\[
\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}{3}+n=\frac{n^2+2}{3}
=\frac{q^2-2q+9}{12}.
\]

Thus
\[
\boxed{
M_r=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{2q(q+1)}{3}, & r\ \text{even},\\[6pt]
\dfrac{2q(q+1)}{3}+\dfrac{q^2-2q+9}{12}, & r\ \text{odd}.
\end{cases}}
\]
